deep.reconstruction:
The page has three short formula lines and one large figure. There is no derivation to follow, so what follows records what is written and the most plausible reading. Interpretive parts are marked [mine].

(1) u_1 = ∫ φ(z_1, s_1) dz_1 + ··· . A quantity u_1 is defined as a line integral, in the variable z_1, of a function φ of two complex arguments z_1 and s_1, plus further terms that are not written.

[mine] In the figure, s_0 and s_1 label the first pair of curves and z_0 and z_1 label the second pair. So s and z appear to be two complex variables (or two sheets/coordinates). Each is carried from an initial value (s_0, z_0) to a final value (s_1, z_1) along a chain of overlapping discs. u_1 would then be an integral of a function of two linked variables, such as an algebraic relation F(s,z)=0, taken along such a path. This is the setting of abelian-type integrals or of functions defined by integrals.

(2) ψ(z, p_1, p_2, …). This is a function of a variable z and a sequence of parameters p_1, p_2, … .

(3) 𝔷 = ψ_1(z, p_1, …). A new (fraktur) variable 𝔷 is defined as a parameter-dependent function of z. [mine] This reads as a change of variable or uniformising substitution whose coefficients depend on parameters (moduli). One would then study how u_1, or the integrand, depends on the p_i.

(4) Figure. Starting at s_0 (bottom left), a chain of four overlapping closed curves runs left to right. The first two overlap, with s_0 and s_1 marked on their lower boundaries. The second and third touch or intersect near z_0. The last large curve carries z_1 at its bottom. A small circled mark inside the last curve probably indicates a singular point (excluded point / branch point). There are hatching marks in the overlap region of the third and fourth curves.

[mine] This is the standard picture of analytic continuation by a chain of overlapping discs (circles of convergence), each disc avoiding the singular point. Both the value of the integral and the function continue from s_0/z_0 to s_1/z_1. The next page, with circles drawn around the points 0, 1, 2, ∞ on a line, continues the same theme. There, continuation of a function with singular points at 0, 1, (2), ∞ is done by overlapping discs, as in Riemann's treatment of the hypergeometric/P-function or of algebraic functions.

The previous page (a biharmonic/elastic plate problem with u+vi, x=±a, y=±b) appears unrelated in content. This page is a separate jotting.

deep.surprise_reason: The page holds only notational fragments and a standard sketch of analytic continuation by overlapping discs. That idea is fully present in Riemann's published dissertation (1851) and his Abelian-functions work (1857). Nothing here goes beyond known Riemann material, and there is too little content to infer anything new.
